The fire god, acting as the mediator between humans and gods in rituals.
The god of death and justice.
The legendary sage credited with compiling the Vedas and Puranas.
The progenitor of humanity and ruler of each Manvantara.
A devotee of Vishnu who attained the status of the pole star.
The genre of 18 major Hindu encyclopedic scriptures.
The supreme goddess, representing cosmic energy and female divinity.
The solar deity, source of light and life.
Ritual fire sacrifices and offerings.
Cosmic age cyclical divisions (Satya, Treta, Dvapara, Kali).
A creator patriarch (Prajapati), son of Brahma.
Universal cosmic order and righteous duty.
The preserver deity of the Hindu trimurti, major deity of Vaishnava Puranas.
The creator deity of the Hindu trimurti.
The elephant-headed deity of wisdom and remover of obstacles.
The god of war, son of Shiva and Parvati.
The king of the gods and ruler of Svarga (heaven).
The god of oceans, waters, and cosmic law.
The cosmic creation process described in the Sarga sections of Puranas.
Avatara of Vishnu, supreme deity, ally of the Pandavas, and teacher of Arjuna.
Third Pandava prince, the archer disciple of Sri Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.
Eldest Pandava prince, known for his adherence to truth and righteousness.
Second Pandava brother, known for his colossal physical strength.
Fourth Pandava prince, twin of Sahadeva, known for his beauty and expertise with swords.
Fifth Pandava prince, twin of Nakula, renowned for his wisdom and astrological skills.
The princess of Panchala, common wife of the five Pandava brothers.
Great warrior and ally of Duryodhana, son of Surya and Kunti.
The eldest son of Dhritarashtra and leader of the Kaurava faction.
The blind king of Hastinapura, father of the Kauravas.
Half-brother of Dhritarashtra and Pandu, prime minister of Hastinapura, famous for his wisdom.
The grand patriarch of the Kuru dynasty, commander of the Kaurava army.
The royal preceptor and teacher of military arts to both Pandavas and Kauravas.
A family preceptor of the Kurus who fought on the Kaurava side.
King of Hastinapura, younger brother of Dhritarashtra, father of the Pandavas.
The capital city of the Kuru kingdom, over which the war is fought.
The capital city built by the Pandavas in the forest of Khandavaprastha.
The island city ruled by Krishna.
Action and its corresponding consequences.
The great 18-day battle between the Pandavas and Kauravas.
The monumental Sanskrit epic detailing the history of the Kuru dynasty.
The sacred battlefield where the Mahabharata war and Gita dialogue occur.
Liberation from the cycle of samsara.
The spiritual path of love, devotion, and surrender to the Divine.
Prince of Gandhara, maternal uncle of Duryodhana, architect of the game of dice.
The celestial abode of Lord Vishnu.
The divine sage and messenger of the gods.
The benevolent demon king who offered three paces of land to Vamana avatar.
The sacred city of Shiva, center of pilgrimage.
A great sage and king who attained the status of Brahmarishi through asceticism.
Vedic solar deity of friendship, contracts, and alliances, closely associated with Varuna.
The physical and moral order of the universe that gods and humans must follow.
The oldest of the four Vedas, containing hymns to the deities.
The cosmic giant or primeval being from whose sacrifice the universe was created.
The goddess of dawn, bringing light and life to the world.
The twin horsemen, divine physicians who rescue and heal.
Vedic solar deity representing the morning sun, associated with the Gayatri mantra.
The deified sacred plant and drink of immortality offered in Vedic rituals.
The earth goddess, consort of Dyaus Pita.
The storm deities, companions of Indra and sons of Rudra.
A saintly prince, devotee of Vishnu, saved from his demon father Hiranyakashipu.
Cosmic era ruled by a specific Manu, consisting of 71 Mahayugas.
The sacred mountain abode of Lord Shiva.
One of the Saptarishis (seven great sages), preceptor of Ikshvaku dynasty.
The sacred river deity, who descended from heaven to purify souls.
The Veda of melodies and chants chanted by Udgatri priests.
The exiled prince of Ayodhyá, son of Dasaratha, and a hero of the Ikshváku race who searches for his abducted wife, Sítá.
The daughter of Janak (Videhan Queen) and wife of Ráma, who is lured by a magic deer and abducted by RávaG.
The loyal younger brother of Ráma who accompanies him in exile and serves as his guardian and confidant.
The ten-necked Rákshas king of Lanká who abducts Sítá through guile and force.
A fiend who transforms into a wondrous golden deer to lure Ráma away from Sítá, leading to her abduction.
The noble vulture king and friend of Dasaratha who dies heroically while attempting to rescue Sítá from RávaG.
The Vánar king and son of the Sun, exiled by his brother Báli, who forms a sacred alliance with Ráma on Mount Rishyamúka.
The son of the Wind-God and chief counselor to Sugríva, who approaches Ráma and LakshmaG as an envoy.
A misshapen, headless giant (formerly the Gandharva Danu) who is released from a curse by Ráma and directs him to seek Sugríva.
An aged, pious votaress and pupil of Matanga who waits for Ráma's arrival before ascending to heaven.
The powerful elder brother of Sugríva and son of Indra, who usurped Sugríva's throne and wife.
The deceased King of Ayodhyá and father of Ráma, whose decree sent Ráma into exile.
The Eternal Father and Creator who decreed the events leading to the giants' overthrow.
The God of Wind and father of Hanumán.
The magnificent island city and fortress of RávaG, surrounded by the ocean.
The mountain where Sugríva and his ministers hide from Báli and where the alliance with Ráma is formed.
A beautiful lake and brook where Ráma laments for Sítá and encounters Sugríva's envoy.
The forest region where Ráma dwelt in exile and where he slew the giant Khara and his host.
A sacred grove once inhabited by Saint Matanga and his pupils, where Savarí maintains her hermitage.
The formal alliance between Ráma and Sugríva, witnessed by the sacred fire.
The epic narrative detailing the life and adventures of Ráma.
Monarch of Ayodhya and father of Rama, Bharat, Lakshmana, and Shatrughna.
attributes.state: Grief-stricken by the exile of his son

attributes.description: Ruler of Mithila and father of Sita and Urmila.
attributes.legacy: Guardian of the Great Bow of Rudra

attributes.description: Dasaratha's youngest queen who demands Rama's exile and Bharat's throning.
attributes.motivation: Securing her son's future at the urging of Manthara

attributes.description: A hump-backed slave-born handmaid who plots against Rama.
The 'Rama with the Axe' who challenges Rama and is eventually debarred from heavenly worlds.
Also known as Shiva, the bearer of the bow broken by Rama at Mithila.
The resistless power described by Rama as the reason for his sudden change in fortune.
The capital of the Ikshvaku dynasty.
The wild forest where Rama is sentenced to spend 14 years in exile.
Rama strings and snaps the celestial bow of Shiva, winning Sita's hand.
Kaikeyi's demand for Bharat's kingship and Rama's 14-year banishment.
The sky father deity, oldest deity of the Vedic pantheon.
The Veda of prose mantras and ritual formulas.
The Veda of spells, charms, and everyday procedures.
Matriarch of the Kuru dynasty, wife of King Shantanu, mother of Vyasa.
Son of Dronacharya, powerful warrior and survivor of the Kurukshetra War.
The sacred dialogue spoken by Krishna to Arjuna before the Kurukshetra War.
First consort of Shiva, who self-immolated at her father Daksha's sacrifice.
A fierce manifestation of Shiva created to destroy Daksha's sacrifice.
A terrifying manifestation of Shiva associated with destruction and protection.
Sage blessed with eternal youth, saved from Yama by Shiva.
The sacred mountain home of Lord Shiva.
The fourteen cosmic realms of the universe.
The four cosmic eras: Satya, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali.
The creation of the universe by Brahma.
The dissolution of the cosmos.
The churning of the cosmic ocean to obtain Amrita (nectar of immortality).
The sacrificial ritual hosted by Daksha that ended in destruction.
Genre of eighteen major sacred texts detailing cosmology, genealogies, and myths.
The deceased King of Ayodhyá, father of Ráma, Bharat, LakshmaG, and Śatrughna. He died of a broken heart following Ráma's exile.
The chief queen of King Daśaratha and mother of Ráma. She is depicted as a prostrate, lustreless star in her grief.
A queen of Daśaratha and mother of LakshmaG and Śatrughna.
The son of Kaikeyí, staying in Rájagriha with his maternal grandfather during the king's death.
The chief household priest who manages the transition of power and sends envoys to fetch Bharat.
The King of Kekaya and Bharat's maternal grandfather.
Also called Girivraja, the capital of Kekaya where Bharat and Śatrughna were residing.
A state of anarchy where no law is known, the strong prey on the weak like fish, and religious/social order collapses.
A prophetic nightmare where Bharat saw his father falling into a lake of mire, drinking oil, and heading south in an ass-drawn chariot.
The process of preserving the king's body in a cask of oil until Bharat's return.
A spirit possessing the strength of a thousand elephants, cursed to be a man-eating monster.
The Supreme Lord who took the form of a Dwarf to defeat King Bali.
A celebrated saint who cursed Tá aká and Márícha.
A holy river born from Brahmá's will, flowing from Lake Mánas.
Also known as Siddháshrama; the site of VishGu's penance and Vi[vámitra's sacrifice.
The sacred, mind-born lake of Brahmá located near Mount Kailása.
The gambling match between Yudhishthira and Shakuni which led to the exile.
The childless monarch of Ayodhyá who decrees a great sacrifice to obtain sons.
The holy hermit and son of VibháGdak who guides the specific sacrificial forms of the Ashvamedha.
The chief queen of Da[aratha who participates in the rites, including the symbolic slaying of the steed.
The kingdom ruled by King Janak, an old ally of Da[aratha.
The Sacrifice of the Steed, involving 21 sacrificial stakes and 300 victims to ensure the king's sovereignty and offspring.
The second rite begun by Rishya[ring using Atharva texts specifically to win sons for the king.
The sacred scriptures (including Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva) that govern the ritual laws.
The King of Míthilá and ally invited to the sacrifice.
The King of the Angas invited to participate in the gathering.
A high-souled hermit residing at Prayág near the confluence of the Gangá and Yamuná.
Another name for the river Yamuná, personified as the Sun-born Goddess.
A holy mountain with varied peaks, located ten leagues from Prayág, chosen as Ráma's forest home.
The sacred confluence where the Yamuná and Gangá rivers meet.
The forced exile of Ráma from Ayodhyá due to Kaikeyí's wish.
The sacred Hindu texts (Vedas) prescribing religious rites and social duties.
A virtuous sage whose hermitage Ráma visits and who directs Ráma to Agastya.
A hermit who follows Ráma and explains the mystery of the Panchápsaras lake.
A great votary who created the Panchápsaras lake through his rites and was seduced by five nymphs.
A holy hermit living south of SutíkshGa’s retreat, whose home Ráma visits first.
A demon who took the form of a ram to kill Bráhmans, eventually devoured and destroyed by Agastya.
A fierce demon who spoke Sanskrit to trick Bráhmans; he was consumed to dust by Agastya's glance.
The Lord divine (Indra) who provided Ráma with a sunbright shaft and an endless quiver.
The 'Lake of the Five Nymphs,' created by MáG akarGi, featuring a hidden palace beneath the waters.
The 'best of hills' that bowed its crest at Agastya's command to allow the sun's journey.
The saintly crowd and hermits of the wood who sought Ráma's protection from fiends.
Fiends or giants of the wood who torment hermits and devour bleeding flesh.
A king of the Ikshváku line who sought a human victim for his sacrifice.
The middle son of Richíka who sold himself as a sacrificial victim and was saved by Vi[vámitra's hymns.
A sacred lake where Vi[vámitra performed his austerities and met Zunah[epha.
The highest spiritual rank sought by Vi[vámitra, requiring total control over rage and desire.
King of the Nishádas and Ráma's ally; he assists Bharat in locating Ráma's hermitage.
The holy river flowing near the Chitrakúma mountain.
The ritual offering of water for the deceased King Daśaratha.
The 'First of Bards' and author of the Rámáyan; a holy hermit and saint who receives the story from Nárad.
A divine saint and son of Brahmá, known as the eloquent messenger of the Gods and inventor of the víGá.
The sacred epic poem that tells the deeds of Ráma, intended to free the world from sin.
Also known as Krita Yuga; a period of truth and perfection that returned during Ráma's reign.
The individual soul or self, which is immortal and distinct from the body.
The ultimate impersonal reality or supreme cosmic spirit.
The spiritual path of knowledge and discrimination between the real and unreal.
The three qualities of nature: Sattva (purity), Rajas (activity), and Tamas (inertia).
Personal duty or right action aligned with one's nature and social position.
The spiritual path of love, devotion, and surrender to the Supreme Lord.
The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.
Selfless or desireless action performed as an offering to the Divine.
The spiritual path of action performed without attachment to results.
The younger brother of Ráma and Bharat, who accompanies Bharat on the journey to the forest.
The royal charioteer and counselor who manages the logistics of the march.
The town on the banks of the Gangá ruled by King Guha.
The supreme deity mentioned in the context of his triple step in the Vamana (dwarf) avatar.
The wild and vast forest where Ráma must spend his fourteen years of exile.
The nectar of immortality mentioned in the context of the struggle between Gods and Daityas.
A demon slain by Indra, mentioned to symbolize the victory of good over evil.
Charioteer and advisor to Dhritarashtra, endowed with divine vision to narrate the war.
The cosmic form of Lord Krishna containing the entire universe revealed to Arjuna.
An ancient king whose fall from heaven is used as a metaphor for Da[aratha's distress.
The supreme duty and religious foundation cited by Kaikeyí to bind the king.
The auspicious planetary hour and lunar sign for the intended consecration.
The aged, saintly wife of Atri who performed ten thousand years of penance and gifted Sítá celestial cosmetics and robes.
A high-souled hermit whose hermitage Ráma visits after leaving Chitrakúta.
A giant demon and brother of RávaG who dwells in Janasthán and harasses the hermits.
The town where Bharat establishes his seat of government to avoid ruling from the capital.
Gold-wrought emblems of Ráma's authority, placed on the throne by Bharat.
The planned ceremony to install Ráma as the Regent Heir to the throne of Ayodhyá.
The field of experience, referring to the material body and mind.
The knower of the field, representing the soul or conscious witness.
The inverted cosmic banyan tree representing material manifestation in Chapter 15.
Divine descent or incarnation of God on earth to restore dharma.
Second Kaurava prince, loyal helper of Duryodhana who insulted Draupadi.
Queen consort of Dhritarashtra, who blindfolded herself out of devotion to her husband.
Mother of the three elder Pandavas and Karna, queen of Pandu.
The sage composer of the Mahabharata, father of Pandu and Dhritarashtra.
Krishna's mission to Hastinapura to negotiate a peaceful settlement, rejected by Duryodhana.
The three scriptural pillars of Vedanta: Upanishads, Brahma Sutras, and Bhagavad Gita.
The philosophical texts concluding the Vedas (Vedanta), focusing on Atman and Brahman.
The momentous exit of Ráma, Sítá, and LakshmaG from Ayodhyá, marked by cosmic omens and city-wide mourning.
The royal saint whose penance brought the river Gangá from heaven to earth to liberate the sons of Sagar.
The deity who received Gangá on his head and quaffed the Halahala poison during the churning of the sea.
A saint who drank the Gangá in anger but later released her through his ears, becoming her symbolic father.
The ancient king whose sixty thousand sons were reduced to ashes and later liberated by Gangá's water.
Wife of Ka[yap and mother of the Titans who performed penance to birth a son capable of slaying Indra.
Wife of Ka[yap and mother of the Gods (Suras).
The wife of Gautam who was cursed to remain invisible and subsist on air until Ráma's arrival.
A powerful ascetic who cursed both Indra and his wife Ahalyá for their betrayal.
A beautiful city built by King Vi[ála, compared to heaven itself.
The cosmic ocean churned by Gods and Titans to obtain the Amrit.
